good.rex: Drive restored on second attempt. First attempt flooded a cold injector. Fuel lost. Acceptable.
good.chip: Restart on attempt two! The bonus exhaust light show is complimentary! The fuel it burned was not!
good.ajoy: Second try. The first one skipped a step, which is the step I mentioned. Drive runs, though.

poor.aria: The drive is in limp mode, but it's still going! Slow and steady! Very slow! Very steady!
poor.marv: The sequence never took. Half power, a coil banging its mount, days added to the leg. We arrive. Eventually, dented.
poor.rex: Restart failed. Drive in limp mode. Coil damaging its mount. We continue at reduced speed. Late.
poor.chip: Limp mode activated! Half the power, all of the warning lights! Days late, with a complimentary dent!
poor.ajoy: It didn't take. Limp mode the rest of the leg, and the coil's denting its mount. I did say in order.

perfect.narrative: Every contact in the order the board called it, first pass. The drive catches at once and settles back into its hum, and the ship sounds like itself again. Your hands did that.

good.narrative: The sequence takes on the second try. The first one dumped a slug of fuel through a cold injector and lit the exhaust up like a festival. The drive runs. The fuel gauge is quieter about it than everyone else.

poor.narrative: The sequence won't take. The drive drops into limp mode: half power, a warning light nobody can switch off, and a coil that bangs against its mount every few minutes until the mount gives a little. You make the rest of the leg at a crawl, days late, with a dent to show for it.

choices.text: Engineer powers down the coil and rebuilds it

outcome.narrative: The engineer shuts the coil down cold, strips it on the deck plate and rebuilds it from the windings out, reciting part numbers like a prayer. It comes back up smoother than it left the yard. Nobody asks how long it had been wrong.

choices.text: Limp mode: half power the rest of the way

outcome.narrative: You drop the drive to half power and leave the fault where it is. It holds. Everything takes twice as long, and the hum has a stutter in it now that everyone pretends not to hear.

choices.detail: Adds days, but the drive holds.

science_link.text: The ship computer appends the reading: keeping a drive alive far from any shipyard is half of what spaceflight is.
science_link.label: How spacecraft engines work

title: The Aphid Census

ai_flavor.aria: Baby aphids are born with babies inside them! That's SO efficient! ARIA is impressed! ARIA is a LOT impressed!
ai_flavor.marv: MARV confirms it: many aphids are born carrying the next generation already. A small colony doubles in days. He would like to deal with this today rather than next week, when there will be considerably more of them.
ai_flavor.rex: REX counts four hundred hostiles, unarmed, multiplying. He respects the strategy. He does not respect the aphids.
ai_flavor.chip: CHIP's Pest Protect Plus would have prevented this! It was canceled at launch! CHIP has never felt so vindicated!
ai_flavor.ajoy: AJOY says soapy water works and costs water. Hands work and cost time. Leaving them costs the crop. She mentions that last one because it's the one you were about to pick.

body:
There are aphids in the growbay.

Small, green, soft and patient, clustered under the leaves in their hundreds, quietly drinking the crop. Yesterday there were a few. Today there are a great many more, and the ones you squash first thing are replaced by lunch. The botanical database has a note on this, which the ship computer reads out without being asked: aphids are born already pregnant.

choices.text: Spray the bay with soapy water

outcome.narrative: You mix soap into {cost.water} points of water and spray every leaf, top and bottom. The aphids hate it. So, briefly, does the crop, which wilts a little and then recovers. By evening the colony is gone. The growbay smells faintly of washing-up for a week.

choices.text: Pick them off by hand

outcome.narrative: Two days of the whole crew in the growbay with tweezers and a jar, leaf by leaf. It is the most boring work anyone has done this voyage. It works. Somebody keeps a tally on the wall. The final count is four thousand and eleven, and nobody wants to talk about it.

choices.text: The botanist sets sticky traps

outcome.narrative: {crew.botanist} hangs yellow sticky cards between the rows, because aphids can't resist the color, and by morning the cards are green with them and the colony is gone. The botanist is quietly smug about it all day.

choices.text: Leave them for now

outcome.narrative: You leave them. The aphids do not leave you. By the next stop the leaves are curling and sticky, and the crop has lost ground it will have to win back.

science_link.text: Many aphids are born already pregnant: the next generation is developing inside them, so a small colony can explode in days.
science_link.label: Aphids

alt_bodies:
The undersides of the leaves have gone green and crowded.

Aphids: soft, slow, patient, packed in their hundreds and drinking the crop one sip at a time. There were a few yesterday. There are a lot today. You squash a cluster after breakfast and it has been replaced by lunch. The ship computer, unprompted, reads out the relevant entry from the botanical database: aphids are born already pregnant.

The growbay has aphids, and the aphids have plans.

They sit in green clumps under the leaves, soft as overripe peas, sucking the sap out of the crop without hurry. Every morning you clear a few leaves. Every afternoon those leaves are full again. The ship computer reads out a line from the botanical database that nobody asked for and nobody can now forget: aphids are born already pregnant.

title: Webs Under the Lamps

ai_flavor.aria: Tiny spiders! Making tiny webs! ARIA loves a craft project! The crop is hosting them, which is so generous of the crop!
ai_flavor.marv: MARV identifies spider mites. Not true spiders, and not insects at all: arachnids, very good at dry, warm growbays. Humidity slows them. Darkness slows them. Their own predators stop them.
ai_flavor.rex: REX cannot see the enemy. He can see the webs. He is treating the webs as the enemy's flag.
ai_flavor.chip: CHIP can confirm that the grow lamps are rated 'Pest Neutral'! CHIP has read the fine print! It says 'neutral' means 'we don't take sides'!
ai_flavor.ajoy: AJOY says wet the air or dim the lights. Or find out what eats mites, which she'd have looked into before running the lamps at full for weeks. But sure.

body:
Fine webs are spreading across the crop.

Under the grow lamps, where it is warm and dry, something too small to see is spinning silk between the leaves and draining them pale. Spider mites. They love dry heat. The growbay's lamps have been giving them exactly what they love, at full power, for weeks.

The leaves they've reached are stippled with tiny yellow dots, like a bad photograph.

choices.text: Mist the bay until they drown in comfort

outcome.narrative: You run the misters day and night for two days and let the humidity climb until the growbay drips. Mites hate wet air. They stop spreading, then stop altogether. It costs {cost.water} points of water, and the crop has never looked so dewy.

choices.text: Lights out for two days

outcome.narrative: You switch off the grow lamps and let the bay go dark and cool. The mites stall without the heat, and two days later the webs are empty. The crop stalls too, and comes back a little behind where it was.

choices.text: The xenobiologist releases predator mites

outcome.narrative: {crew.xenobiologist} brings out a vial from the specimen hold: a predatory mite that eats spider mites and nothing else. They let a few hundred loose among the rows. Before long the webs are empty and the predators, with nothing left to eat, simply die out. 'Elegant,' says the xenobiologist, and means it.

choices.text: Ride it out

outcome.narrative: You let them run. The webs spread across half the bay before the mites burn through their own food and crash, and the crop is left pale and stippled. It will recover. It will take a while.

science_link.text: Farmers fight spider mites with another mite, Phytoseiulus persimilis, which eats them and almost nothing else.
science_link.label: Predatory mites

alt_bodies:
There is silk on the crop.

Thin, dusty webbing hangs between the leaves under the grow lamps, and beneath it something too small to see is sucking the leaves pale. Spider mites. They thrive in dry heat, and for weeks the growbay lamps have been running hot and dry around the clock, which is to say the ship has been building them a resort.

The leaves they've reached are freckled with tiny yellow dots.

The crop looks dusty. It is not dust.

Up close, under the warm glare of the grow lamps, fine webs are strung leaf to leaf, and the leaves under them are paling, pricked all over with tiny yellow dots. Spider mites: too small to see one at a time, very easy to see all at once. They love warm, dry air, and the lamps have been making nothing else for weeks.

title: In the Ducts

ai_flavor.aria: They're EVERYWHERE! ARIA can hear them in the vents! ARIA doesn't have ears! ARIA can hear them anyway!
ai_flavor.marv: MARV traces fungus gnats from the growbay soil into the ventilation. The scrubbers are losing about a point of efficiency a day. The source is the soil. Clearing the ducts without clearing the bay buys time, nothing more.
ai_flavor.rex: REX has sealed the bridge vent with tape. The gnats came in through the door. He has taped the door. He is reassessing.
ai_flavor.chip: CHIP regrets that ventilation pest removal is not covered by your service plan! It is covered by the premium plan! The premium plan is also full of gnats!
ai_flavor.ajoy: AJOY says it has to be all at once: the bay and the ducts together, or they come back. Every way of doing that costs something. She'd have said so when it was only the soil, but nobody asked then.

body:
The pests have left the growbay.

Tiny black gnats, bred in the damp soil, have found the air vents, and the air vents go everywhere. They are in the galley, the bunks, the bridge. Worse, they are in the scrubbers: the air recyclers are clogging with their bodies, and the oxygen readings, for the first time this trip, are drifting the wrong way.

Every breath aboard has a faint, small, buzzing aftertaste.

choices.text: Seal the growbay and fumigate the ship

outcome.narrative: You seal everyone forward, fumigate the growbay and the ducts for two days, then scrub the air clean again. The gnats are gone. So is a good share of the air, spent purging the ship, and the crew's patience, spent sleeping in a corridor.

choices.text: Vent the growbay to vacuum

outcome.narrative: You open the growbay to space for ninety seconds. Every gnat in it goes out with the air. So does a good deal of the soil moisture, and the crop, which was not built for vacuum, takes a beating it will take weeks to recover from. The ducts clear by themselves once the source is gone.

choices.text: The engineer flushes the ducts with hot air

outcome.narrative: {crew.engineer} reroutes engine heat through the ventilation and runs it hot enough to cook every gnat in every duct, and bakes the top inch of the growbay soil under the lamps. Two days, some fuel, a ship that smells of toast. Not one gnat survives.

choices.text: Live with it

outcome.narrative: You live with it. The scrubbers keep clogging, the air keeps thinning, the crop keeps losing ground, and everyone aboard learns to eat with a hand over their plate. The gnats die back on their own by the next stop. Nobody misses them.

alt_bodies:
The growbay's problem is now everyone's problem.

The gnats that hatched in the damp soil have found the vents, and the vents lead everywhere: bunks, galley, bridge. They have also found the scrubbers, which are clogging with tiny black bodies, and for the first time this voyage the oxygen readout is creeping down instead of holding.

There is a gnat in every cup of coffee and, it feels like, every breath.

There are gnats on the bridge. That is the first sign the infestation has outgrown the growbay.

Small, black and born in damp soil, they have taken the ventilation and spread through the whole ship. The worst of it is in the air scrubbers, where they have died in drifts, and the clogged scrubbers are losing ground: the oxygen readings are drifting the wrong way.

Nobody eats with their mouth open any more.

title: Every Drop

ai_flavor.aria: We can recycle EVERYTHING! ARIA has seen the whiteboard! ARIA has framed the whiteboard!
ai_flavor.marv: MARV notes the recycler, at full output, recovers most of what the crew uses, including the parts nobody mentions. It tastes of recycler. It is water.
ai_flavor.rex: REX reports the water reserve is a threat to mission readiness. He also reports the recycler is a threat to morale. He is choosing between threats.
ai_flavor.chip: CHIP would like to introduce RECLAIM™, the ship's own artisanal water! Bottled on board! From sources! CHIP won't say which sources!
ai_flavor.ajoy: AJOY notes the space station back home has drunk its own recycled water for decades without anyone drawing a whiteboard about it. She'd just like it known she isn't the squeamish one here.

body:
The water gauge is low enough that the ship computer has started announcing it at breakfast.

There are ways to stretch it. Every one of them is, in its own way, about recycling something nobody wants to think about recycling. Someone has put up a whiteboard. The whiteboard has a diagram. The diagram has arrows, and the arrows go places.

choices.text: Run the recycler at full tilt

outcome.narrative: You run the water recycler at full output for a day. It gives back clean, safe, faintly metallic water from places best not described at the table. The crew drinks it. The crew describes it at the table anyway.

choices.text: Wring the water out of the air

outcome.narrative: Two days of running the dehumidifiers flat out and draining the condensate into the tanks. Every breath anyone takes puts a little water into the air, and now it is going back where it came from. The ship ends up very dry and slightly crackly with static.

choices.text: Give the crop less

outcome.narrative: You turn the crop's share of the water down. The crew gets more; the crop gets less, and the growbay gets very quiet about it. The orders stand until you change them back.

science_link.text: The International Space Station recycles around 98% of its water, including the crew's sweat and urine, into drinking water.
science_link.label: Water recycling in space

title: Ice on the Scope

ai_flavor.aria: ICE! Delicious, frozen, wonderful ICE! ARIA would like all of it! ARIA understands that is not a plan!
ai_flavor.marv: MARV puts the ice at roughly eighty percent water by mass. A detour to mine it properly costs fuel and two days. Drones get less of it, faster. A good pilot could match its spin and scoop it in one pass.
ai_flavor.rex: REX has checked the ice for hazards. It is cold. It is tumbling. It is not hostile. He is making an exception.
ai_flavor.chip: CHIP can't sell you this ice! Nobody owns it! CHIP is devastated! CHIP is also thirsty, by association!
ai_flavor.ajoy: AJOY says fill the tanks if you can afford the detour. If not, take what the drones can carry. 'Push on' is also an option, in the sense that it is listed.

body:
Long-range sensors have found something in reach that is worth more than gold right now: a chunk of ice.

It is a dirty, tumbling lump about the size of a house, a loose piece of some comet's long-ago breakup, drifting a few hours off your heading. It is mostly water. The tanks are mostly not.

The question is how much of it you can bring aboard, and what you'll spend getting there.

choices.text: Detour and mine it properly

outcome.narrative: Two days alongside the tumbling ice with the cutters and the scoops. It comes aboard in gray blocks and melts down clean. Fifteen points of water for four of fuel. The tanks gurgle happily all evening.

choices.text: Send the drones for what they can carry

outcome.narrative: The drones go out, chip what they can, and come back heavy. Eight points of water for two of fuel, and no time lost to the detour. The rest of the ice tumbles on without you.

choices.text: The pilot matches its spin and scoops it

outcome.narrative: {crew.pilot} brings the ship alongside, matches the ice's slow tumble exactly, and holds it there while the scoops bite. One pass. Twelve points of water. The pilot pretends this was easy. It was not easy.

choices.text: No time. Push on

outcome.narrative: You let it go. The ice tumbles away on the scope, full of exactly what the ship is short of, and everyone watches it go. The water gauge goes on being low.

title: The Drive Is Complaining

ai_flavor.aria: The engine is SINGING! ARIA doesn't think it's a happy song! ARIA thinks it's the other kind!
ai_flavor.marv: MARV has the drive running hotter every leg it stays at PLAID. Nothing has failed. Things that run this hot for this long tend to stop not failing.
ai_flavor.rex: REX recommends easing off. He does not like recommending easing off. He likes the alternative less.
ai_flavor.chip: CHIP must remind you that PLAID is rated for 'short bursts of enthusiasm'! This is not a short burst! This is a lifestyle!
ai_flavor.ajoy: AJOY says one notch down and the noise stops. Or keep it, and keep someone in the engine room with it. Ignoring a kettle is also a choice. Not one she'd make.

body:
Too long at PLAID, and the drive has started to make a new noise.

It is not a loud noise. It is a thin, high, steady whine somewhere aft, under the usual roar, like a kettle that has been left on in another room. The engine room is hotter than it should be. The coolant gauge is in the yellow and leaning toward the next color. Every so often the deck plates tick, as if something under them is counting.

choices.text: Ease off to LUDICROUS

outcome.narrative: You ease the drive down a notch. Within an hour the whine is gone, the coolant gauge drifts back to green, and the deck plates stop counting. The crew sleeps better. The schedule slips a little. Everyone agrees it's a fair trade.

choices.text: Keep PLAID, with the engineer babysitting the drive

outcome.narrative: {crew.engineer} moves a cot into the engine room and nurses the drive through the next leg by hand, bleeding a little fuel into the coolant loop to keep the temperatures down. The whine never quite goes away. The engineer doesn't sleep much. You stay at PLAID.

choices.text: Keep PLAID and ignore it

outcome.narrative: You keep the drive flat out and ignore the noise. The noise doesn't ignore you. Somewhere mid-leg a mounting bracket aft cracks with a bang that everyone hears, and a piece of hull goes with it. The whine carries on as if nothing happened.

title: Redline

ai_flavor.aria: Everything is RED! The alarms are RED! The engine is RED! ARIA would like one thing that isn't red please!
ai_flavor.marv: MARV gives the injector housing minutes, not legs, at this temperature. A hand rebalance can bring it back without a shutdown. Done badly, it costs more than the shutdown would have.
ai_flavor.rex: REX has cleared the engine room of everyone not essential. That was everyone. He has let the engineer back in.
ai_flavor.chip: CHIP regrets that the PLAID package's 'Unlimited Thrills' clause has a limit! You have found it! Congratulations on your thrills!
ai_flavor.ajoy: AJOY says rebalance the injectors by hand, now, while it's still a repair and not a salvage job. She said 'ease off' two alarms ago, but this works too.

body:
The drive alarm has been going for ten minutes, and the drive has been at PLAID for longer than the manual's footnote likes to think about.

The engine room is a wall of heat. The coolant is boiling in its lines. Something in the injector housing has started to glow a color that the manual describes only as 'see a technician'. The nearest technician is aboard, and has just arrived, and is looking at it with an expression nobody wants to see on a technician.

It has to come down now. The question is how hard.

choices.text: Rebalance the injectors by hand

briefing.aria: The injector housing is glowing! Rebalance the injectors in order and we can cool this right down!
briefing.marv: The housing has minutes at this temperature. Rebalance the injectors in sequence. Done badly, it costs more than a shutdown.
briefing.rex: Injector housing critical. Engine room is cleared. Rebalance in sequence. Every mistake scorches frame.
briefing.chip: You've found the limit of Unlimited Thrills! Rebalance those injectors in order! Burns are not a covered thrill!
briefing.ajoy: Rebalance them in order, now, while it's a repair and not salvage. I said 'ease off' two alarms ago. Anyway.

perfect.aria: First pass! The temperature fell like a stone and the drive is purring at LUDICROUS! Barely a scorch!
perfect.marv: First pass, a foot from the housing. A little scorched hull, a little fuel, and LUDICROUS. Cheaper than any shutdown.
perfect.rex: Injectors rebalanced first pass. Temperature down. Minor hull scorch. Drive holding at LUDICROUS.
perfect.chip: Perfect rebalance! Your drive is back at LUDICROUS! Ask about renewing the PLAID package! Maybe later!
perfect.ajoy: Clean, first pass, and the drive purrs at LUDICROUS. I'd have eased off sooner, but fine. Good hands.

good.aria: The second injector put up a fight, but you won! LUDICROUS speed, with a little cough! We'll call it character!
good.marv: The second injector resisted long enough to scorch the frame. LUDICROUS restored, with a cough it will keep.
good.rex: Second injector resisted. Frame scorched. Drive restored at LUDICROUS with a cough. Monitor it.
good.chip: LUDICROUS restored! The cough is a premium feature! Frame scorch is a known PLAID side effect!
good.ajoy: The second injector got away from you and the frame paid. Drive's at LUDICROUS. With a cough. Just noting the cough.

poor.aria: It took a few tries, but the drive came back at LUDICROUS! Let's give the engine room a nice long rest!
poor.marv: Wrong twice before right. Half the aft frame cooked. LUDICROUS, eventually. A shutdown would have cost less.
poor.rex: Two failed passes. Aft frame heavily damaged. Drive restored at LUDICROUS. Engine room off-limits.
poor.chip: Three tries, one cooked aft frame, one LUDICROUS drive! Frame damage is excluded under 'Unlimited Thrills'!
poor.ajoy: Wrong twice before it was right, and half the aft frame cooked meanwhile. It's not a salvage job. Barely.

perfect.narrative: Every injector rebalanced in order, first pass, with the housing glowing a foot from your hands. The temperature falls like a stone. Two points of hull where the housing scorched, three of fuel bled into the restart, and the drive comes back at LUDICROUS, purring, as if it had never complained in its life.

good.narrative: The second injector fights you and the housing scorches the frame before you get it. Eight points of hull, six of fuel, and the drive comes back at LUDICROUS with a cough it will keep for a while.

poor.narrative: The rebalance goes wrong twice before it goes right, and by then the housing has cooked half the aft frame. Fourteen points of hull, ten of fuel. The drive comes back at LUDICROUS, eventually, and nobody wants to be in the engine room for a week.

outcome.narrative: You strip the injector cover and go in by hand.

choices.text: Crash-stop and drop to LIGHT SPEED

outcome.narrative: You kill the drive hard and let it cool to a crawl, then bring it back at LIGHT SPEED and leave it there. Four points of hull from the thermal shock. The schedule takes the real hit: you'll fly slow until someone decides to risk it again.

choices.text: The engineer rebuilds the injector housing

outcome.narrative: {crew.engineer} shuts the drive down properly and rebuilds the injector housing from spares over four long days, while the ship drifts. It comes back better than new, at LUDICROUS. Six points of fuel to restart a cold drive, and four days the schedule did not have.

choices.text: Push through at PLAID

outcome.narrative: You keep it at PLAID. The alarm keeps going. Halfway through the leg the injector housing lets go with a sound like a cathedral bell, and the aft frame takes twelve points of damage before the drive stabilizes on its own, somehow, still at PLAID. Nobody is proud of this. Everybody is still alive.

title: Yellow From the Bottom Up

ai_flavor.aria: The bottom leaves are going yellow! ARIA thinks yellow is a lovely color! ARIA has been told it is not a lovely color for leaves!
ai_flavor.marv: MARV has run the nutrient feed through the analyzer. Nitrogen is low enough that the plant has started taking its oldest leaves apart for spares. MARV respects the logistics. He would prefer they stopped.
ai_flavor.rex: REX has located the shortage. It is chemical. He has been told he cannot requisition chemicals from the crew. He has been told why. He has stopped asking.
ai_flavor.chip: CHIP's NitroBoost™ pellets would fix this overnight! They are back on Earth! In a warehouse! Next to everything else CHIP recommended!
ai_flavor.ajoy: AJOY says the plant isn't sick so much as hungry, which anyone could have seen if the feed had been refreshed. Feed it from the crew, the galley or the botanist's notebook. Each one costs someone something.

body:
The yellow starts at the bottom.

The oldest leaves of the {crop.name} have gone the color of weak tea, while the new growth at the top stays green and keeps asking for more. It is not a disease. It is a budget. The plant is short of nitrogen, and it is doing what anyone on a short budget does: taking from the old to feed the young.

The growbay's nutrient feed has been recycled so many times that it is mostly water with a memory. Something has to go back into it.

choices.text: Feed it the crew's urine

outcome.narrative: You divert the urine line from the water reclaimer into the nutrient tank, diluted the way the manual says, on a page nobody expected to read. Urine is mostly water, salt and urea, and urea is nitrogen with good intentions. Within the week the new leaves come in dark and the old ones stop surrendering. The reclaimer gets less back. The crew is told at dinner. Dinner ends early.

choices.text: Dissolve ration bars into the feed

outcome.narrative: You crumble ration bars into warm water and let them steep into a brown broth that smells like a regret. Given time, the bacteria in the growbay's filters break protein down into ammonium, which a root can use. The {crop.name} drinks it gratefully. The galley does the sums on what it gave up and keeps them to itself.

choices.text: {crew.botanist} rebuilds the feed from scratch

outcome.narrative: {crew.botanist} drains the tank, tests it, and rebuilds the feed from the growbay's mineral stock and a notebook of ratios kept since training. The nitrogen comes back into balance and the yellow stops climbing. 'It wasn't sick,' the botanist says. 'It was hungry. Those are different conversations.'

choices.text: Let it feed on itself

outcome.narrative: You let the plant carry on borrowing from itself. It is very good at this, right up until there is nothing old left to borrow from. The yellow climbs a little higher each morning.

science_link.text: Nitrogen moves inside a plant, so a starving plant strips it from its oldest leaves to feed new growth: the yellowing climbs from the bottom up.
science_link.label: Nitrogen deficiency

title: Standing Water

ai_flavor.aria: ARIA has been watering the crop extra to cheer it up! ARIA has been asked to stop! ARIA is having a complicated afternoon!
ai_flavor.marv: MARV logged the blocked drain last week and filed it under plumbing. He has refiled it under botany. The roots did not wait for the paperwork.
ai_flavor.rex: REX has secured the drain. It surrendered a fistful of roots. He is keeping them as evidence.
ai_flavor.chip: CHIP must point out that the AquaFlow™ drain warranty excludes 'organic obstruction'! CHIP asked what that means! CHIP regrets asking!
ai_flavor.ajoy: AJOY says stop watering first, which she'd have said days ago if anyone had asked why a watered plant looked thirsty. Then air, scissors or peroxide. The brown roots are gone already; it's the white ones you're saving.

body:
The {crop.name} has looked thirsty for days, so the crew has been watering it more. It has not helped.

Under the beds, a drain has been blocked all that time, and the root trays have been sitting in still water. Roots need air as much as leaves need light. Starved of it, they have gone brown and soft, and a water mold has moved in to finish the job. The plant wilts because its roots can no longer drink, while standing up to its ankles in water.

The growbay smells like a pond that has given up.

choices.text: Clear the drain and let the beds dry

outcome.narrative: You clear the drain, a plug of root, soil and something best not named, and let the trays empty back into the reclaimer. Then you water nothing for days, which feels wrong every single morning. Slowly the surviving roots firm up and go white again. The rotten ones don't come back. They were never going to.

choices.text: Trim the rot and repot by hand

outcome.narrative: Every plant comes up, every brown root comes off with clean scissors, and every plant goes back into fresh, dry medium. It is slow and filthy, and the smell gets into everyone's sleeves. What goes back in is smaller and cleaner, and it starts drinking again within the week.

choices.text: {crew.engineer} pipes air into the root trays

outcome.narrative: {crew.engineer} clears the drain, then runs a spare air line from the scrubbers into the root trays and drills it full of holes. The water fizzes. Roots that were drowning get their air back, and the mold, which likes things still and airless, does not. The pump runs off the drive bus for a while, and the fuel gauge notices.

choices.text: Pour a medkit's peroxide through the roots

outcome.narrative: You dilute the medkit's hydrogen peroxide and pour it through the root trays. It fizzes against the rot, kills the mold, and leaves oxygen behind as it breaks down. Growers have done this for generations. Medics have opinions about it. The roots go white again within days.

choices.text: Keep watering. It looks thirsty

outcome.narrative: You water it more, because it looks thirsty, because it is thirsty, because its roots are drowning. The water goes straight into the problem. By the next stop the stems are soft at the base and the growbay smells worse.

science_link.text: Roots breathe. Waterlogged soil starves them of oxygen, and water molds such as Pythium move into the weakened roots, so the plant wilts while standing in water.
science_link.label: Root rot

title: Too Much Light

ai_flavor.aria: The lamps are on FULL! It's like summer in there! ARIA loves summer! The crop has asked ARIA to stop saying summer!
ai_flavor.marv: MARV notes the lamps have been at maximum since the dimmer failed. A leaf can only use so much light. The top of the crop has been receiving the rest, and is complaining in the only format it has.
ai_flavor.rex: REX recommends cutting the enemy's light. He has been reminded the lamps are ours. He recommends it anyway.
ai_flavor.chip: CHIP is proud to report the SunMax™ lamps are running at FULL CAPACITY! CHIP has been told that is the problem! CHIP is less proud!
ai_flavor.ajoy: AJOY says shade it, switch it or fix it. The bleached leaves are done either way; the new ones can still be saved. She'd have checked the dimmer a week ago. Just saying.

body:
The grow lamps' dimmer has failed, and it has failed bright.

The lamps have been running flat out for days, a little closer to noon than any noon has ever been. The top leaves of the {crop.name} have gone pale and papery, bleached in patches the color of old newspaper. The lower leaves, in the shade of the upper ones, look perfectly fine and slightly smug.

A plant can only use so much light. Past that, the extra does damage, and the leaves at the top have been taking all of it.

choices.text: Rig shade cloth from the bedsheets

outcome.narrative: Every spare sheet aboard goes up under the lamps, pinned with tape and hope. The light beneath them drops to something a leaf can work with, and the new growth comes in green. The crew sleeps under jackets for the rest of the leg and mentions it.

choices.text: Switch the lamps by hand, around the clock

outcome.narrative: Without a dimmer the only settings are on and off, so somebody turns them on and off: some light, some dark, around the clock, by hand, by alarm. The average works out to something kinder. The bleached leaves stay bleached. The new ones don't.

choices.text: {crew.engineer} fixes the dimmer

outcome.narrative: {crew.engineer} pulls the dimmer board, finds a relay welded shut by its own enthusiasm, and swaps in the one from the galley toaster. The lamps settle back to a working noon. The toaster now does only off and on, and the crew learns to live with both.

choices.text: Light is food. Leave it

outcome.narrative: You leave the lamps on full on the reasoning that light is food. Light is food the way a firehose is a drink. The pale patches spread down another row of leaves before the plant starts dropping them.

science_link.text: Too much light damages the machinery of photosynthesis itself: leaves bleach where they catch more than they can use. Plant scientists call it photoinhibition.
science_link.label: Photoinhibition

title: Small White Clouds

ai_flavor.aria: It's SNOWING in the growbay! Upward! ARIA has never seen upward snow! ARIA has been informed the snow is bugs!
ai_flavor.marv: MARV identifies whiteflies, which are neither entirely white nor, strictly, flies. They are, however, everywhere. MARV accepts half of the name.
ai_flavor.rex: REX has engaged the cloud repeatedly. It dispersed each time. It reformed each time. He considers this a stalemate. He does not accept stalemates.
ai_flavor.chip: CHIP's HoverHoover™ Pro has a dedicated pest attachment! It is not aboard! The regular vacuum is aboard! CHIP supposes it will have to do!
ai_flavor.ajoy: AJOY says vacuum them, dazzle them with foil or chill them out. Leaving them costs the crop, and the mold comes after. She's listing that so nobody can say she didn't.

body:
Brush a leaf of the {crop.name} and a small white cloud lifts off it.

Whiteflies: tiny, powdery, moth-like things that live on the undersides of leaves, drink the sap, and leave behind a sticky honeydew that a black mold then grows on. They are poor flyers. They don't need to be good ones. Every time someone walks past, the cloud lifts, settles, and goes back to drinking.

For a moment each time, the growbay looks as if it is snowing upward.

choices.text: Vacuum the undersides, leaf by leaf

outcome.narrative: You fit the narrowest nozzle to the ship's hand vacuum and go row by row, flipping leaves and hoovering. Whiteflies fly badly and lift easily, which makes them perfect for this. The canister fills with something that looks like lint and isn't. By the end the leaves are clean, and the vacuum has been retired from household duties.

choices.text: Line the beds with foil from the hull insulation

outcome.narrative: You peel a sheet of reflective insulation off the cargo bay wall and lay it silver side up across the soil. Whiteflies find their plants by looking for green against a dark ground; light bouncing up from below confuses them, and they wander off to die somewhere less shiny. The cargo bay is colder now. The beds look like a baked potato.

choices.text: Chill the growbay overnight

outcome.narrative: You let the bay's heat go for a night and a day. Whiteflies are warm-climate insects, and the cold stops them feeding, stops them breeding, and drops them off the leaves; you sweep them up in the morning. The {crop.name} doesn't love the cold either, and loses a little ground.

choices.text: Leave them to it

outcome.narrative: You leave them to it. The honeydew builds up, the black mold follows it, and the leaves beneath can't catch the light. The {crop.name} loses ground. The cloud, when someone walks past, is bigger.

science_link.text: Whiteflies find their host plants by color against the ground. Light reflected up from below confuses them, so growers really do lay reflective mulch under a crop.
science_link.label: Whiteflies

title: Someone Is Writing on the Leaves

ai_flavor.aria: Someone is writing on the leaves! ARIA is trying to read it! ARIA thinks it says 'yum'! ARIA is not sure!
ai_flavor.marv: MARV has attempted to translate the tunnels. They are not language. They are a larva eating in the direction of more leaf. MARV concedes this is also what most writing is.
ai_flavor.rex: REX has located the hostiles. They are inside the leaves. He cannot shoot the leaves. He has never wanted to shoot leaves more.
ai_flavor.chip: CHIP is excited to report that the crop is now Personalized™! Every leaf is one of a kind! CHIP has been asked to stop putting that in the newsletter!
ai_flavor.ajoy: AJOY says a spray won't reach them, in case anyone was reaching for one. Fingers, scissors or a scalpel. The dot at the end of the line is the one you want.

body:
Pale, winding lines have appeared on the leaves of the {crop.name}, as if someone has been doodling on them from the inside.

That is roughly what has happened. Leaf miners: tiny fly larvae that hatch inside a leaf and eat their way through it, between the top skin and the bottom, leaving a tunnel that widens as they grow. A spray can't reach them. They are already indoors.

Hold a leaf up to the lamp and there is a small dark dot at the end of each line. The dot is the author.

choices.text: Pinch the dot at the end of every line

outcome.narrative: You go leaf by leaf with the lamp behind each one, find the dot at the end of each line, and press it between finger and thumb. Every tunnel stops where its author did. It is meticulous, slightly horrible, and it works. The lines stay on the leaves, a story that ends abruptly.

choices.text: Cut off every mined leaf

outcome.narrative: Every leaf with a line on it comes off and goes into the recycler, larvae and all. The {crop.name} is left looking thin and plucked. It will grow the leaves back. The miners will not grow back.

choices.text: {crew.medic} operates

outcome.narrative: {crew.medic} brings a scalpel, a magnifier and the steadiest hands aboard, and performs a very small surgery on every affected leaf: a nick, a lift, a larva out. The leaves heal around the cuts. The medic enters each one in the medical log under minor procedures, and nobody has the heart to object.

choices.text: Let them finish the chapter

outcome.narrative: You let the lines lengthen. In time the larvae finish, drop into the soil and come out as small flies, which lay the next generation in the next leaves. The {crop.name} loses ground, and the doodling carries on in a new hand.

science_link.text: Leaf miners are insect larvae that live and feed inside a leaf, between its upper and lower surfaces; the trail widens as the larva grows.
science_link.label: Leaf miner

title: Hold Music

ai_flavor.aria: The support line is playing MUSIC! ARIA is dancing! The fabricator is still broken! ARIA is dancing anyway!
ai_flavor.marv: MARV estimates the free queue's wait from the hold music's loop count. MARV has stopped estimating. MARV has started humming, which concerns MARV.
ai_flavor.rex: REX does not wait on hold. REX has never waited on hold. REX is on hold.
ai_flavor.chip: CHIP can upgrade you to Priority Support™! It is the same technician! They are just happier to see you!
ai_flavor.ajoy: AJOY says the fault is in the feed, not the firmware. She has said so twice. The support line has not asked her.

body:
The fabricator is broken, and its display has helpfully replaced the error code with a support number.

The manufacturer's line answers on the first ring, which is suspicious, and puts you on hold on the second, which is not. A recorded voice thanks you for your loyalty. A second recorded voice explains that your call is important, in a tone that suggests a third voice will be along later to explain how important.

Meanwhile, nothing on the ship can be made.

choices.text: Pay for priority support

outcome.narrative: Priority support turns out to be a shorter queue with better music, then a real technician who walks you through a firmware rollback in a voice of enormous patience. The fabricator wakes up. The invoice arrives before it has finished booting.

choices.text: Wait on the free line

outcome.narrative: You stay on the free line. The hold music loops until the crew can hum the bass part and does, unprompted, in their sleep. Days later a technician answers, sounds surprised anyone is still there, and talks you through the fix in a few minutes. The fabricator works. The music does not leave.

choices.text: Strip the repair kit for parts

outcome.narrative: You hang up and open the repair kit instead. Its seals, springs and spare feed gear go into the fabricator, and the fabricator goes back to work. The next leak aboard will have to be fixed with something else.

choices.text: {crew.engineer} hangs up and opens it

outcome.narrative: {crew.engineer} hangs up on the hold music mid-chorus, takes the side panel off and finds the feed line packed solid, exactly where nobody on the support line would have looked. The rebuild takes days and comes out better than new. The support line calls back afterwards to ask how they did.

title: Whiskers

science_link.text: The fabricator's beard has a real name: stringing, when molten filament oozes from a printer nozzle as it travels between parts. A worn or dirty nozzle makes it worse.
science_link.label: Fused filament fabrication

ai_flavor.aria: Everything the fabricator makes has a little BEARD! ARIA has named all of them! ARIA has run out of beard names!
ai_flavor.marv: MARV attributes the whiskers to a worn nozzle oozing between moves. It is a small fault. Small faults in machines this worn are what large faults look like early.
ai_flavor.rex: REX does not accept whiskers on equipment. REX has trimmed his sidearm's holster. It did not need trimming. It does now.
ai_flavor.chip: CHIP is pleased to launch Rustic Finish™, a hand-trimmed artisan range! The trimming is by you! The pricing is by CHIP!
ai_flavor.ajoy: AJOY has been trimming the prints with nail scissors. She would like the nozzle changed before she has to buy more nail scissors.

body:
The fabricator still works, but everything it makes now comes out with whiskers.

Fine threads of feedstock trail off every print, as if the nozzle can't quite bear to let go. A bracket arrives looking like it needs a shave. A cup comes out wearing a small beard. The crew has started trimming prints with nail scissors, and there is now a waiting list for the nail scissors.

choices.text: Clean the nozzle by the book

outcome.narrative: Two days of heat cycles, a brass brush and a cleaning filament the manual insists on by brand. The nozzle stops oozing. The next cup comes out clean-shaven, and the wear counter steps back from the edge.

choices.text: {crew.engineer} swaps the worn nozzle

outcome.narrative: {crew.engineer} pulls the old nozzle, holds it up to the light, and shows everyone the hole worn oval. The new one goes in tight. The fabricator prints like it did on its first day, and the nail scissors return to general use.

choices.text: Sweep up the whiskers for feedstock
choices.sub: Some scrap · the fabricator keeps wearing

outcome.narrative: You keep printing and keep the trimmings. Swept off every surface and bagged, the whiskers add up to a respectable bundle of scrap stock. The fabricator keeps wearing, whiskering all the while.

title: Steam in the Engine Room

science_link.text: The ship computer notes that spacecraft really do shed heat this way: with no air to carry it off, the only route out is radiation, so ships carry radiator panels and sometimes use their own skin.
science_link.label: Spacecraft thermal control

ai_flavor.aria: The engine room has its own WEATHER now! ARIA has forecast fog! ARIA was right! ARIA is never right about weather!
ai_flavor.marv: MARV reports the coolant loop losing more each PLAID leg than it can recover. It can be topped up. MARV notes that topping up and fixing are different words for a reason.
ai_flavor.rex: REX has cleared the fog from the engine room twice. It came back twice. REX respects that.
ai_flavor.chip: CHIP's Coolant Club™ delivers fresh coolant monthly! There are no months out here! CHIP will deliver anyway! Somehow!
ai_flavor.ajoy: AJOY says the hull is the best radiator the ship has. It was not built to be one, and it will show it. She'd have just eased off, but she suspects simple isn't the plan.

body:
The engine room has its own weather now.

A warm, thin fog fills it, smelling faintly of coins: the drive's coolant, boiling off at PLAID faster than the loop can win it back. The coolant gauge reads low and falling. Somewhere behind a panel a relief valve hisses every few minutes, like someone deciding not to say something.

The loop can be topped up. It cannot be topped up with nothing.

choices.text: Top the loop up from the water tank
choices.sub: Stay at PLAID · costs drinking water

outcome.narrative: You bleed {cost.water} points of drinking water into the coolant loop. The fog thins, the gauge climbs out of the red, and the relief valve goes quiet. You stay at PLAID. The water tank is the one that pays for it.

choices.text: Ease off to LUDICROUS

outcome.narrative: You bring the drive down a notch and the boiling stops within the hour. The fog clears, the valve stops hissing, and the coolant settles at a level it can hold. The schedule slips, a little and permanently.

choices.text: Let it boil and keep going

outcome.narrative: You leave the drive at PLAID and the coolant to its fate. The fog gets into the air scrubbers, which spend the next leg coughing it out and doing their actual job rather less. The air goes stale. The drive does not care.

choices.text: {crew.engineer} runs the coolant through the hull

outcome.narrative: {crew.engineer} reroutes the loop through the outer plating and turns the whole skin of the ship into a radiator. The heat pours out into the dark and the boiling stops at PLAID. The plating was never meant to be cooked from inside, and some of it buckles.

title: Sympathetic Vibration

science_link.text: Resonance is real: drive any structure at its own resonant frequency and small pushes add up each cycle until something gives. Engineers design to keep those frequencies away from the ones a machine makes.
science_link.label: Mechanical resonance

ai_flavor.aria: The whole ship is HUMMING! ARIA is humming along! ARIA has found the key! It is the key of uh-oh!
ai_flavor.marv: MARV has matched the hum to the hull's resonant frequency. A structure driven at its own frequency stores energy every cycle. Eventually it spends it, all at once, on itself.
ai_flavor.rex: REX has seen a bridge come down this way, on a training film. He did not enjoy the film. He is enjoying this less.
ai_flavor.chip: CHIP regrets that harmonic disassembly is listed under 'acts of physics' in your policy! CHIP did not know physics could act! CHIP is impressed!
ai_flavor.ajoy: AJOY says the note is the problem, not the speed. A little slower is enough to fall off it. A lot slower is for people who want to be sure. She'll let you guess which one she'd pick.

body:
At PLAID, for this many legs, the drive has finally found the note the ship was built around.

The whole hull is humming. Not the drive's usual roar: a deep, even tone that comes up through the deck and into everyone's teeth. Cups walk across tables. A corridor panel has shaken its screws halfway out and is working on the rest. The flight stick is shaking hard enough to make the instruments unreadable.

Things that resonate long enough come apart. The ship would prefer not to find out which things first.

choices.text: Detune: drop to RIDICULOUS

outcome.narrative: You pull the pace back to RIDICULOUS and the hum dies with it, all at once, like a choir told to stop. The schedule takes the loss. The crew spends an hour putting screws back in, in a silence that feels enormous.

choices.text: Brace the ship and ride it out

briefing.aria: The whole ship is humming! Brace through the big shakes, catch every panel, and we ride it out at PLAID!
briefing.marv: The hull is at its resonant frequency, storing energy every cycle. Brace through the peaks. The panels are already walking.
briefing.rex: Resonance across the hull. Everyone on a strut. Brace through the peaks. Do not let the panels go.
briefing.chip: Harmonic disassembly is an act of physics and not covered! Brace the ship and keep it in one piece, please!
briefing.ajoy: Holding PLAID through the hum. Bold. Brace through the peaks, catch the panels. I'd have slowed down, but sure.

perfect.aria: Every panel caught and the hum faded to a buzz! We're still at PLAID! The hull only lost a little paint!
perfect.marv: Every panel caught, eased off the note by a hair. Mostly paint lost. The ship is still in its original number of pieces.
perfect.rex: All loose panels secured. Resonance broken. Minimal damage. PLAID maintained.
perfect.chip: Perfect bracing! PLAID speed, hull intact, just a little paint! CHIP calls that a value proposition!
perfect.ajoy: Off the note by a hair, every panel caught. That's roughly what I meant. Well done, I suppose.

good.aria: We rode it out at PLAID! A few dents and one cracked strut, but the hum is gone!
good.marv: Most panels caught. The rest dented the corridor and a strut cracked aft. We kept PLAID. The hull paid for it.
good.rex: Most panels secured. Corridor dented, aft strut cracked. PLAID maintained. Inspect that strut.
good.chip: PLAID preserved! Corridor dents add character! Strut replacement sold separately!
good.ajoy: The panels you missed dented the corridor, and a strut cracked. Still at PLAID, if that was the point.

poor.aria: We're still at PLAID! Some panels went through a wall and a seam needed a quick patch, but we're in one piece!
poor.marv: Bracing late and out of order. Panels through the wall, an aft seam opened and closed in a hurry. Still PLAID.
poor.rex: Bracing failed. Panels breached a corridor wall. Aft seam opened, sealed. PLAID maintained. Morale down.
poor.chip: Still at PLAID! Panels through walls and an aft seam! Harmonic disassembly remains uncovered!
poor.ajoy: Late and in the wrong order. Panels through the wall, a seam aft. Still at PLAID. I'd have slowed down. Just noting.

perfect.narrative: Every loose panel is caught and strapped as it starts to walk, and the drive is eased off the note by a hair at exactly the right moment. The hum fades to a buzz. The hull loses a little, mostly paint. You stay at PLAID.

good.narrative: Most of the panels are caught. The ones that aren't leave dents in the corridor, and a strut cracks aft before the hum fades. You stay at PLAID, and the hull is the one that pays.

poor.narrative: The bracing goes in late and in the wrong order. By the time the hum fades, panels have gone through the corridor wall and a seam aft has opened and been sealed in a hurry. You are still at PLAID. Nobody feels faster.

outcome.narrative: Everyone grabs a strut. You hold PLAID and fight the hum.

choices.text: {crew.engineer} re-torques every mount

outcome.narrative: {crew.engineer} idles the drive and goes through the ship with a torque wrench and a stethoscope, tightening every mount until the frame stops ringing. Restarting a cold drive costs fuel. When it comes back to PLAID, it comes back without the hum.

choices.text: {crew.pilot} hunts for a quieter speed

outcome.narrative: {crew.pilot} walks the drive down through the hum, notch by fraction, burning fuel on every correction, until the note slides off and fades. It ends one notch below PLAID, at LUDICROUS. The schedule gives a little. The ship stops singing.

title: The Concourse Booth

ai_flavor.aria: The booth is MINT GREEN! Mint green is a healing color! ARIA read that somewhere! ARIA may have written it!
ai_flavor.marv: MARV has pulled the booth's inspection record. It has one. MARV would prefer not to describe it, except to say the date on it is not recent.
ai_flavor.rex: REX has assessed the man at the noodle bar. Steady hands. Clean nails. REX will be standing behind him the entire time.
ai_flavor.chip: CHIP is a proud sponsor of the concourse booth! CHIP is not a proud sponsor of what happens inside it! Those are separate contracts!
ai_flavor.ajoy: AJOY flagged this wound when it happened. She is not going to say so again. She is just going to stand very visibly beside the patient, whichever door you pick.

body:
{patient.name}'s wound has been 'fine' since it happened. At the station it stops pretending. By the time the ship docks there is a fever, and a smell under the dressing nobody mentions.

The station clinic is shut. A sign on the door announces a Staff Wellness Day, and a second sign, in different handwriting, says it has been Staff Wellness Day for some time. What the concourse has instead is a coin-operated surgical booth, painted a reassuring mint, with a slot for payment and a seat with straps.

Also, at the noodle bar, there is a man who says he used to be a nurse.

choices.text: Feed the booth

outcome.narrative: {patient.name} sits, the straps close, and the booth plays a cheerful tune for the whole procedure, which is the worst part. It drains, cleans, doses and dresses the wound with a precision no human hand has ever had or wanted. Then it prints a receipt and asks for a rating.

choices.text: {crew.medic} runs the booth on manual

outcome.narrative: {crew.medic} pries open the booth's service panel, finds its demonstration mode, and talks it through the whole procedure one step at a time, overruling it twice. It takes two long nights and costs nothing but everyone's nerves. {patient.name} comes out mended.

choices.text: Pay the man at the noodle bar in food

outcome.narrative: The man who used to be a nurse turns out to have been one, or to have watched one very closely. He works on {patient.name} at the galley table, slowly and well, and takes {cost.food} points of food for it, packed to go. He does not leave a name.

choices.text: Clean it aboard and push on
choices.sub: No cost now · the patient gets worse

outcome.narrative: You turn down the booth and the noodle bar and clean the wound aboard with what the ship has. It is not enough to mend it, only enough to slow it down. {patient.name} flies on worse off than before, saying it's fine, which nobody believes any more.

title: Property of the Lane Authority

ai_flavor.aria: A buoy! Full of fuel! Just floating there! ARIA is sure the Lane Authority would WANT us to have it! ARIA has not asked them!
ai_flavor.marv: MARV has read the plate. Tampering is an offense. MARV has also read the fuel gauge, which describes a larger offense, and one the vacuum will fine us for.
ai_flavor.rex: REX notes the buoy is unarmed, unmanned and unwatched. He says this in the tone of a man who hopes you will not ask him what he means by it.
ai_flavor.chip: CHIP is pleased to report the buoy accepts all major payment methods! The emergency tariff is very reasonable, for an emergency! That's what makes it an emergency tariff!
ai_flavor.ajoy: AJOY has the lane chart up. If the marker drifts, the next ship through here is a freighter, a few weeks behind you. No pressure. She'll just leave the chart up.

body:
A navigation buoy drifts off the bow, blinking its lane marker into the dark for anyone who might be lost.

It is a squat, sensible machine with a reserve tank to keep its station-keeping thrusters lit for longer than anyone aboard will live, and a plate riveted to its side: PROPERTY OF THE LANE AUTHORITY. TAMPERING IS AN OFFENSE. IN AN EMERGENCY, CALL THE NUMBER BELOW.

The number below has been scratched off. Underneath, in marker, someone has written: 'they don't pick up.'

The buoy's reserve tank is full. Yours is not.

choices.text: Drain the buoy dry

outcome.narrative: You dock with the buoy and empty its reserve into your own tank. The gauge climbs out of the danger band. Behind you the lane marker flickers, steadies, and begins to drift, a little further off its mark with every hour, for whoever comes along the lane next. Nobody aboard says anything about it. Everybody watches it go.

choices.text: Pay the Lane Authority's emergency tariff

outcome.narrative: The buoy has a payment slot, of course. You feed it the tariff and it releases a measured, receipted share of its reserve, prints a thank-you message to your console and goes back to blinking. The fuel is entirely legal. The receipt says so, twice.

choices.text: Bleed off only what it can spare

outcome.narrative: {crew.engineer} talks the buoy's tank controller into running a maintenance purge, the kind it does on schedule anyway, and catches the purge in your lines instead of letting it vent. The buoy loses nothing it would have kept. The lane stays marked. The gauge rises less than anyone hoped, and enough to matter.

choices.text: Leave it blinking

outcome.narrative: You leave the buoy to its work. The lane stays lit behind you, a small steady light for the next ship that comes this way short on luck, and the crew is quietly glad of it. The fuel gauge is exactly as worrying as it was.

title: Water Is Also Propellant

ai_flavor.aria: Water is fuel! Fuel is water! Everything is everything! ARIA has never been prouder of chemistry!
ai_flavor.marv: MARV confirms the chemistry. Every liter split for the drive is a liter nobody drinks. He has put both gauges side by side so nobody can pretend otherwise.
ai_flavor.rex: REX approves of fuel that cannot be stolen, because you are already carrying it. He would like to stop thinking about where else that logic leads.
ai_flavor.chip: CHIP reminds you that HydroBurn™ electrolysis is a premium feature! Your ship came with it anyway! CHIP is investigating how that happened!
ai_flavor.ajoy: AJOY checked the electrolyzers last night. They work. She hasn't run them, since splitting the drinking water is apparently a 'captain decision.' She's looking forward to watching you make it.

body:
The ship computer has found fuel. It is in the water tank.

Split water with enough electricity and you get hydrogen and oxygen, which is what the reserve thrusters burn on a bad day. The computer has drawn a diagram to explain this. The diagram has a cartoon droplet on it, smiling, walking cheerfully into the engine.

Nobody likes the droplet.

choices.text: Crack water into propellant

outcome.narrative: The electrolyzers run for two days and nights, splitting water into gas and piping the gas aft. The fuel gauge climbs. {cost.water} points of water went into it, and the cartoon droplet is removed from the diagram by popular request.

choices.text: Burn some breathing reserve as oxidizer

outcome.narrative: You bleed reserve oxygen into the thruster feed, where it burns a clean, eager blue that would be very beautiful if it were not the air. The fuel gauge rises. Everyone breathes a little more carefully afterwards, which is, on reflection, the point.

choices.text: The pilot flies the leg on attitude jets

outcome.narrative: {crew.pilot} shuts down the main drive and flies the leg on attitude jets and patience, nudging the ship along the cheapest line there is. It saves fuel. It costs the pilot a night's sleep and their entire opinion of attitude jets.

choices.text: Leave the water where it is

outcome.narrative: You keep the water for drinking. The droplet goes back in its folder. The fuel arithmetic stays on the screen a while longer, unchanged, as if waiting for you to change your mind.

science_link.text: The ship computer attaches the chemistry: water splits into hydrogen and oxygen with enough electricity, and serious mission plans would refuel spacecraft from ice found along the way.
science_link.label: Splitting water

title: Falling Past a Giant

ai_flavor.aria: It's SO BIG! And it's going to throw us! For FREE! ARIA loves a planet that gives back!
ai_flavor.marv: MARV has the closest approach timed to the second. He would like it on record that the second is quite short and the planet is quite hard.
ai_flavor.rex: REX has flown slingshots before. He does not describe them. He tightens his harness and recommends everyone do the same.
ai_flavor.chip: CHIP reminds you that gravity is provided free of charge by the planet and is not a CHIP product! CHIP is looking into that!
ai_flavor.ajoy: AJOY says burn at the bottom of the fall, not before. Everyone burns before. She's telling you now so that later it counts as having told you.

body:
A gas giant hangs off the starboard bow, banded in rust and cream, too large for the viewport to hold.

Swing close past something that heavy and you borrow a little of its momentum for free. Fire the engines at the bottom of the fall, at the very closest point, and the same burn buys far more speed than it would anywhere else. The manual calls this efficient. It calls the closest point 'the part where timing matters.'

The planet does not care whether you time it. It is very large and has never needed to.

choices.text: Time the burn at the bottom of the fall

briefing.aria: Here comes the bottom of the fall! Lock onto the closest point and light the burn right there for a free throw!
briefing.marv: Closest approach is a short window on a hard planet. Burn early and we fight its gravity. Late buys less.
briefing.rex: Approaching closest pass. Track the burn point and hold it. Early wastes fuel. Late wastes the planet.
briefing.chip: Free gravity, courtesy of the planet! Lock the burn at the bottom of the fall and pocket the savings!
briefing.ajoy: Burn at the bottom of the fall, not before. Everyone burns before. I'm saying it now so it counts later.

perfect.aria: Right at the bottom! The giant threw us like a stone from a sling, and the tank came out ahead!
perfect.marv: Lit at the deepest point, to the second. We came out ahead on fuel. The planet is unimpressed. I am slightly impressed.
perfect.rex: Burn on the mark. Maximum gain from the assist. Heading locked. Clean slingshot.
perfect.chip: Perfect slingshot! Free speed from a planet that does not invoice! CHIP is still looking into that!
perfect.ajoy: Bottom of the fall, to the second. Exactly where I said. Good, you listened.

good.aria: A little late, but the giant still gave us plenty! Thank you, big planet!
good.marv: A shade late, past the bottom. Less than a perfect burn would buy. Still a profit, which planets rarely offer.
good.rex: Burn slightly late. Reduced gain. Still a positive result. Next time, on the mark.
good.chip: A good slingshot! Not our Platinum slingshot, but still a gain! Planet gravity remains free, for now!
good.ajoy: A shade late. Not before, at least, so half credit for listening. We still came out ahead.

poor.aria: We lit a bit early and scraped through the cloud tops! The belly got a free sandblasting, but we're through!
poor.marv: Early, high on the fall, pushing against the gravity we came to borrow. Less fuel than we started with. Less paint.
poor.rex: Burn premature. Fuel spent against gravity. Cloud-top skim scoured the belly. Hull damage. We are clear.
poor.chip: An early burn! You paid for gravity the planet was giving away free! Belly paint not included!
poor.ajoy: You burned before the bottom. Like everyone. Which is why I told you. Less fuel and a scoured belly now.

perfect.narrative: The burn lights at the deepest point of the fall, to the second, and the ship comes out the far side of the giant flung onto its heading like a stone from a sling. The tank comes out well ahead. The planet, receding, looks exactly as unimpressed as before.

good.narrative: Close enough. The burn lights a shade late, past the bottom of the fall, and buys less than a perfect one would have. It still buys plenty. The giant shrinks behind you, still banded, still enormous, still not interested.

poor.narrative: The burn lights early, high on the fall, and the ship spends fuel shoving against the very gravity it came to borrow. You skim lower to make up for it, through the edge of the cloud tops, and come out with less fuel than you went in with and the paint scoured off the belly.

outcome.narrative: You take the ship down toward the cloud tops and wait for the moment.

choices.text: Take the long, lazy orbit

outcome.narrative: You let the giant take its time with you: a wide, patient loop, no burn to speak of, the planet's pull doing all the work. It is free fuel, paid for in days. The giant fills the viewport for so long that the crew stops looking at it, which nobody would have believed at the start.

choices.text: The pilot flies the fall by hand

outcome.narrative: {crew.pilot} flies the fall by hand, so low that the cloud tops slide past like a floor, and lights the burn at the bottom without once looking at the computer. The ship comes out on its heading with fuel to spare. The pilot spends the evening explaining how easy it was to anyone within range.

choices.text: Skim the cloud tops with the intakes open

outcome.narrative: You drop into the giant's upper atmosphere with the intakes open and scoop hydrogen like a whale taking krill. It works. The tank fills. The hull, which was never designed for weather of any kind, comes out the other side scorched, buffeted and a good deal thinner in places.

science_link.text: The ship computer appends the physics: a burn made at the lowest, fastest point of a fall buys the most speed, the Oberth effect, and real probes pair it with gravity assists past giant planets.
science_link.label: The Oberth effect

title: Feed Grade

ai_flavor.aria: Oats! Mostly! ARIA thinks 'mostly' is a lovely word! It leaves room for surprises!
ai_flavor.marv: MARV has read the label twice. The calories are real. The 'something else' is listed as 'binder'. MARV has elected not to look it up.
ai_flavor.rex: REX has scanned the freighter. It is a cattle bus with a drive. REX stands down, slightly offended to have been asked.
ai_flavor.chip: CHIP notes that NutriLoaf™ is also mostly oats! NutriLoaf™ costs more! That's the NutriLoaf™ difference!
ai_flavor.ajoy: AJOY has checked the pellets against the medical database. They won't hurt anyone. She'd have bought real food at the last station, but fine. Fry them.

body:
A bulk freighter overtakes you on the lane, hails, and asks whether you would like to buy some feed.

It is hauling animal fodder to a ranching colony: pressed pellets, sealed by the tonne, stamped NOT FOR HUMAN CONSUMPTION on the front and, in smaller letters on the back, BUT IT WON'T KILL YOU. The freighter's master has seen your drive plume and done the arithmetic everyone does when they see a ship running lean.

'It's mostly oats,' they say. 'And something else. Mostly oats.'

choices.text: Buy a pallet, fair and square

outcome.narrative: You pay, they pass a pallet across on a line, and the galley fills with a smell that is mostly oats. Fried, it is edible. Fried with salt, it is nearly good. The ranching colony will never know what it lost.

choices.text: Swap fuel for feed

outcome.narrative: Out here the freighter's master would rather have fuel than gold. You pump some across and a pallet comes back the other way. The pellets are mostly oats. The fuel was entirely fuel. It seemed like a fair trade at the time, and may yet.

choices.text: Lend them the engineer for two days

outcome.narrative: {crew.engineer} spends two long days aboard the freighter fixing a cargo crane that has been jammed since the last colony, and comes back smelling of hydraulic fluid and oats, towing a pallet of feed as payment. Fair's fair, says the master. Mostly oats.

choices.text: Thank them and decline

outcome.narrative: You thank the freighter and decline. It pulls ahead, unhurried, carrying enough fodder for a whole ranch, and the galley goes back to counting what's left. Somebody mentions the oats at dinner. Nobody laughs.

title: Something in the Flour

ai_flavor.aria: The flour is ALIVE! That's basically sourdough! ARIA has named the biggest one!
ai_flavor.marv: MARV has estimated the weevil population. He will not share the figure. He will say it is larger than the crew, by a margin that is not close.
ai_flavor.rex: REX has declared the dry stores a hostile position. He has not yet worked out how a person surrenders to a beetle.
ai_flavor.chip: CHIP's records show the grain was certified pest-free at loading! The certificate is also in the sack! It has been partly eaten!
ai_flavor.ajoy: AJOY noticed the sacks settling weeks ago and assumed it was the grain. It wasn't the grain. In her defense, nobody else noticed anything at all.

body:
The dry stores are moving.

Weevils: small, brown, patient beetles that came aboard as eggs inside the grain and have spent the voyage turning the reserve sacks into something that looks like flour and is mostly beetle. They are not dangerous. They are simply everywhere, they have eaten a real share of what was left, and they are still going.

What remains can be saved. None of the ways of saving it are pleasant.

choices.text: Sift it, bake it, call it protein

outcome.narrative: You sift out what can be sifted and bake the rest, weevils included, into a dense brown bread that is, as the ship computer points out, higher in protein than it has ever been. The stores stretch. Dinner is eaten in a silence that has a texture.

choices.text: Heat-treat the sacks against the drive

outcome.narrative: You stack the sacks against the drive housing and run it warm for days, until nothing in the flour is alive to argue. Heat is the old cure for weevils, and it works, at the price of the fuel it took to make the heat and the days it took to wait. What comes out is plain, sifted, entirely dead flour. It has never looked so good.

choices.text: The chef makes a feature of it

outcome.narrative: {crew.chef} declares the weevils an ingredient, roasts them separately with salt and the last of the paprika, and serves them beside the bread like croutons. It takes a long day in the galley and a great deal of persuasion. By the end of the week people are asking for extra.

choices.text: Space the lot and start clean

outcome.narrative: Every sack goes out of the airlock, beetles and all, and the hold is scrubbed down to the metal. Nobody has to eat a weevil. The stores are {cost.food} points of food smaller, and the captain who gave the order is, for one evening, extremely popular.

science_link.text: The ship computer attaches the reference: grain weevils lay their eggs inside the kernels, so a sealed sack can hatch its own infestation, and heat or deep cold is how stored grain is treated.
science_link.label: The wheat weevil

title: Green, Lightly Salted

ai_flavor.aria: It's a SALAD! A liquid salad! ARIA has always wanted to drink a salad!
ai_flavor.marv: MARV confirms the culture is edible, nutritious and able to keep a crew alive. He has also read the tasting notes. He recommends salt.
ai_flavor.rex: REX has eaten worse in the field. He does not specify. Nobody asks him to.
ai_flavor.chip: CHIP notes that GreenGains™ algae smoothies sell for a fortune on Earth! You have a whole tank! CHIP is drafting a franchise agreement!
ai_flavor.ajoy: AJOY has been giving the culture a little extra light for weeks. In case. Nobody thanked her then. She is accepting thanks now.

body:
Behind the life-support panel, in a tank nobody has opened since launch, the backup algae culture has been quietly doing its job: drinking light, breathing out oxygen, and growing.

It has grown a great deal. It is a thick, bright, faintly alarming green, and according to the manual it is also food: complete protein, vitamins, everything a body needs, in a form no body has ever wanted.

The tank's maintenance tag reads HARVEST IF REQUIRED. It is required.

choices.text: Skim the tank down to the glass

outcome.narrative: You skim the culture down to the glass. It comes out as a green paste with the texture of wet felt and a taste best described as 'pond'. It is extremely nutritious. With the culture cut back, the backup air supply makes less backup air, and the O2 gauge says so.

choices.text: Crop it a little each day

outcome.narrative: You crop the culture a little each day, never more than it can replace, so the tank keeps breathing while it feeds you. It is slow, careful farming of the least appetizing crop aboard. It costs days. It costs nothing else.

choices.text: Feed it to the growbay instead

outcome.narrative: Algae makes a fine fertilizer. You stir a bucket of it into the growbay's soil loop and the plants perk up within the day. The galley is no fuller, but the crop is thriving, and the crop is the reason anybody is out here.

choices.text: Leave it to make air

outcome.narrative: You close the panel. The culture goes on doing what it was put there to do. The air stays good, the stores stay low, and the green tank glows faintly behind its panel like a pantry somebody locked.

science_link.text: The ship computer attaches the reference: green algae such as chlorella have been studied for decades as a way to feed a crew and refresh its air at the same time.
science_link.label: Chlorella, food and air

title: The Coolant Is Water

ai_flavor.aria: There's water in the engine! The engine has been HIDING water! ARIA feels betrayed and also thirsty!
ai_flavor.marv: MARV has the coolant loop's volume. It would help. He also has the drive's temperature without it. That would not.
ai_flavor.rex: REX advises against draining coolant in a hostile sector. He has checked. The sector's only hostile feature is the thirst.
ai_flavor.chip: CHIP reminds you that CoolFlow™ coolant is rated for 'incidental contact'! CHIP is checking whether drinking it counts as incidental!
ai_flavor.ajoy: AJOY says the loop can spare ten points, not all of it, and the drive runs hot after unless you ease off to LIGHT SPEED. She'd ease off. She'd also have said so sooner, if anyone had been holding the valve.

body:
Someone has noticed that the drive's coolant loop is, chemically speaking, mostly water.

It is filtered, deionized, treated and plumbed through the hottest parts of the ship, and there is a good deal of it. The manual says the loop must never be drawn down in flight. Everybody's dry mouth says otherwise.

Take water from the loop and the drive runs hotter. Something will have to give: the pace, the hull, or the argument.

choices.text: Draw it down and ease off to LIGHT SPEED

outcome.narrative: You draw off what the loop can lose and drop the drive to LIGHT SPEED, where it runs cool enough not to miss it. The tanks are fuller. The ship is slower, and will stay slower until you decide to risk it again. The stars, as usual, are in no hurry either.

choices.text: Draw it down and keep the pace

outcome.narrative: You draw off the coolant and leave the drive at speed. It runs hot, then hotter, and the frame around the drive housing pays for it, warping and ticking its way through the leg. The tanks are fuller. The aft bulkheads have a new curve to them.

choices.text: Swap in the reserve coolant

outcome.narrative: {crew.engineer} isolates a section of the loop, drains it into the drinking tank and backfills it from reserve coolant canisters nobody remembered were aboard. The gauges argue for two days, then settle. The drive never notices. The water tastes faintly of metal and is very welcome.

choices.text: Leave the loop alone

outcome.narrative: You leave the coolant where the manual wants it. The drive runs cool and sweet and indifferent, and the water tanks stay where they were, which is low. Everyone drinks a little less and looks at the coolant pipes a little more.

science_link.text: The ship computer appends the reference: water is one of the best coolants there is, which is why so many reactors and engines run on it, and why taking it out has consequences.
science_link.label: Water as a coolant

title: Water from the Fuel Cells

ai_flavor.aria: The power units make WATER! And we've been throwing it away! ARIA is going to drink a glass of electricity!
ai_flavor.marv: MARV has the exchange rate: fuel in, water out, a little warmth for the trouble. He would call it poor, if the alternative were not worse.
ai_flavor.rex: REX approves of a system that makes its own drinking water. He has opinions about who left the box unticked. He is holding them in reserve.
ai_flavor.chip: CHIP notes that RECOVER was a premium setting in the original configuration! It has been unlocked as a goodwill gesture! The goodwill invoice follows!
ai_flavor.ajoy: AJOY flagged that box at launch. Nobody ticked it. Since nobody asks: flat out is six of fuel for ten of water, ticking over is two of fuel for five and takes two days. She'd have had the water since launch.

body:
The auxiliary power units are fuel cells, and fuel cells have a side effect the ship computer has only now thought to mention.

Feed them hydrogen and oxygen and they make electricity, a little heat, and water: pure, clean, warm water, trickling out of an exhaust line into a waste tank that has been venting it overboard since launch, because nobody ticked the box marked RECOVER.

The box is now ticked. The question is how hard to run them.

choices.text: Run the cells flat out

outcome.narrative: You run the auxiliary cells flat out and route the exhaust into the drinking tank. Water trickles in, warm and pure and faintly smug. The fuel it took to make it is gone for good. On balance, it is easier to fly short of fuel than short of water.

choices.text: Let them tick over for two days

outcome.narrative: You let the cells tick over for two days and nights, sipping fuel and dripping water, and by the second morning the tank is a little fuller and the fuel gauge has barely moved. It is the most restful fix anyone aboard has ever made.

choices.text: Run a fuel cell from cargo through them

outcome.narrative: You plug a spare fuel cell from cargo into the auxiliary loop and let its whole charge run through into water. The cell comes out empty and the tank comes out fuller. It is, technically, the most expensive drink in the sector. Nobody minds.

choices.text: Keep the cells on standby

outcome.narrative: You leave the fuel cells on standby. The water stays low, the fuel stays in the fuel tank where the manual likes it, and the box marked RECOVER stays ticked, for whatever good it does a machine that isn't running.

science_link.text: The ship computer attaches the history: the fuel cells that powered the Apollo spacecraft and the Space Shuttle made the crew's drinking water as a by-product.
science_link.label: Fuel cells and their water

title: Oxygen Candles

ai_flavor.aria: Candles that make AIR! It's like a birthday party where everyone gets to keep breathing!
ai_flavor.marv: MARV has the candles' chemistry. They are reliable, mostly. MARV notes that 'mostly' is the word that ended up in the incident report on the old Mir station.
ai_flavor.rex: REX has located the fire extinguisher, the fire blanket and the second fire extinguisher. He is holding all of them.
ai_flavor.chip: CHIP notes the candles are BreathEasy™ brand and well past their best-before date! The warranty has also expired! Unlike the candles, the warranty cannot catch fire!
