ai_flavor.ajoy: AJOY has read the card twice, which is twice more than anyone else aboard. One at a time, every time, with somebody watching. She'd underline it, but it's already in bold.

body:
In the emergency locker, under years of dust and a laminated card nobody has read, there is a crate of oxygen candles.

They are canisters of chemical that burns hot and slow and gives off breathable oxygen as it goes: the last-ditch air of submarines and old space stations. The crate's expiry date has passed. The card says, in bold, LIGHT ONE AT A TIME, IN A FIREPROOF HOLDER, AND NEVER LEAVE IT UNATTENDED.

Next to the words there is a little drawing of a flame, crossed out. It is not reassuring.

choices.text: Burn them one at a time, by the book

outcome.narrative: You burn them one by one in the fireproof holder, someone on watch beside each candle from the first spark to the last gray ash. It takes days of shifts, and nobody sleeps near the locker. The air thickens back into something you don't have to think about.

choices.text: Light the whole crate at once

outcome.narrative: You light the whole crate in the cargo bay and stand well back. The candles burn fast and very hot, and one of them, past its date, spits a jet of molten slag across the deck before anyone can reach it. Someone takes a burn putting it out. The air comes back all at once, thick and warm. The deck has a new scar.

choices.text: The engineer builds a proper burner

outcome.narrative: {crew.engineer} builds a proper burner out of a coolant jacket and a length of exhaust pipe, feeds the candles through it one after another with the heat dumped into the hull, and keeps a fire blanket over one shoulder the whole time. It takes two days instead of four, and it is tidy and slightly terrifying to watch. The air comes back.

choices.text: Leave them in the locker

outcome.narrative: You close the locker. Expired chemical fires are a last resort, and this is not the last of anything yet. The air stays thin. The candles stay where they are, waiting, as they have for years, for things to get worse.

science_link.text: The ship computer attaches the record: chemical oxygen generators keep submarines and space stations breathing in emergencies, and in 1997 one started a serious fire aboard the Mir space station.
science_link.label: Oxygen candles

title: The Oxygen Generator Sulks

ai_flavor.aria: The air machine is having a little rest! ARIA understands! ARIA would just like it to rest a bit faster!
ai_flavor.marv: MARV has cataloged every fault code the generator can display. There is one. MARV considers this a design philosophy rather than a fault.
ai_flavor.rex: REX has threatened the generator. It did not respond. REX respects that, and intends to keep trying.
ai_flavor.chip: CHIP notes that AirWorks™ Premium Support could diagnose this remotely! Remote support requires a working air supply on your end! CHIP will hold!
ai_flavor.ajoy: AJOY has seen this fault before. It's always the membrane. She has told the generator so. It doesn't listen to her either.

body:
The oxygen generator has stopped generating.

It is the unit that splits water into breathable oxygen and spare hydrogen, and it has gone into a protective shutdown over something it refuses to name. Its display shows a single amber light and the word FAULT, which is all it ever shows, for every fault, in a manner that suggests you should already know.

The restart sequence is in the manual. It is long. It must be done in order.

choices.text: Run the restart sequence by hand

briefing.aria: The air machine is napping! Its restart sequence is long, but if we do it in order it'll wake right up!
briefing.marv: Oxygen generator in protective shutdown. One fault code, as always. The restart is long and must be done in order.
briefing.rex: O2 generator offline. Restart sequence from the manual. Every step, in order. No improvising.
briefing.chip: AirWorks™ Premium Support is on hold, so you're the support! Run the restart in order and keep breathing!
briefing.ajoy: It's the membrane, it's always the membrane, but the restart is what we've got. In order. All of it.

perfect.aria: Green light! The generator is turning water into air again and the O2 curve is going up! Big breaths, everyone!
perfect.marv: Every step in order, first time. Green light. The generator resumes making air. I'll stop rationing my breathing.
perfect.rex: Generator restored first pass. O2 production nominal. Good execution.
perfect.chip: Green light, first time! Fresh air is back! AirWorks™ Premium would have charged you for that!
perfect.ajoy: Green, first time. It was probably the membrane, but the sequence did it. Fine. Nicely done.

good.aria: We had to start over once, but the light went green! The generator's a little grumpy, but it's making air!
good.marv: Lost our place, started over, got green anyway. It runs a little under its old rate. It holds grudges.
good.rex: Restart on second run. Generator below previous rate. Output sufficient. Monitor.
good.chip: Restarted! A touch below factory rate! AirWorks™ Performance Tuning can fix that, once we have a signal!
good.ajoy: You lost your place and had to start over. Green anyway, a bit slower. Still the membrane, I bet.

poor.aria: It's running! Slowly! It has a brand new fault code too, which is exciting! The air is getting a little better!
poor.marv: It kept tripping. Now it runs at a fraction of its rate with a code not in the manual. The air improves, slightly.
poor.rex: Restart failed repeatedly. Generator at reduced output. Unknown fault code. Air improving, marginally.
poor.chip: Partial restart! With a bonus mystery fault code! AirWorks™ would love to diagnose it! Remotely! Someday!
poor.ajoy: It kept tripping the shutdown. It runs, slowly, with a new code nobody can find. I'd have checked the membrane.

perfect.narrative: Every step in order, first time. The amber light blinks, considers, and turns green, and the generator settles back into its long patient work of turning water into air. By the second evening the O2 curve has turned the right way up.

good.narrative: You lose your place and have to start over, but the light goes green in the end. The generator restarts grudgingly, a little under its old rate, as if it has not entirely forgiven you.

poor.narrative: The sequence trips the protective shutdown again, and again, and when it finally restarts it runs at a fraction of its rate with a new fault code nobody can find in the manual. The air improves a little. The mood does not.

outcome.narrative: You open the manual at the restart sequence and start at the top.

choices.text: Force it on in emergency mode

outcome.narrative: You skip the diagnosis and force the generator back on in emergency mode, which splits water as fast as the pumps can feed it and wastes a good deal doing so. The air comes back quickly. The tank pays {cost.water} points of water for the speed, and the amber light glares the whole time.

choices.text: The engineer strips it down

outcome.narrative: {crew.engineer} takes the generator apart on the galley table, finds a hairline crack in a membrane, replaces it from spares and puts everything back together over several careful days. It runs better than it has in months. The amber light, for once, has nothing to say.

choices.text: Live on the reserve tanks for now

outcome.narrative: You leave the generator sulking and draw on the reserve tanks. Nothing gets better. Nothing gets worse yet, either. Everybody aboard has started breathing in the slow, deliberate way people breathe when they are thinking about it.

science_link.text: The ship computer attaches the reference: the International Space Station makes its oxygen the same way, by splitting water, and still carries older backups for the days the generator won't.
science_link.label: Making oxygen in orbit

title: Load-Bearing Furniture

ai_flavor.aria: We're redecorating! On the OUTSIDE! ARIA has always said this ship needed an open-plan layout!
ai_flavor.marv: MARV has costed every fitting aboard by weight of usable plate. The galley table is worth the most. MARV has not put it on the list. MARV is capable of mercy, occasionally.
ai_flavor.rex: REX would strip his own bunk first. He has offered. It is on the list.
ai_flavor.chip: CHIP must point out that the bunk partitions are leased! The lease does not cover use as hull plating! CHIP has added a small fee, for creativity!
ai_flavor.ajoy: AJOY says the racks will grow back faster than trust in the bunk room. She'd start with the racks, and ask whoever tends the growbay first. Not that the list was hers to draw up.

body:
The hull needs plating, and the stores don't run to plating. The ship, on the other hand, is full of metal. It is just that all of it is currently being something else.

There are the partitions between the bunks. There are the growbay's spare racks. There is the galley table, which is the only thing aboard everyone agrees about. All of it unbolts. All of it would make a decent patch.

The ship computer has drawn up a list of what could go. It has, tactfully, left the galley table off it.

choices.text: Strip the partitions between the bunks

outcome.narrative: The partitions come down and go up again on the outer hull, cut and bent and welded over the worst of the damage. The hull holds better. The bunk room is now one long open dormitory where nobody gets a moment to themselves, and everyone has opinions about it.

choices.text: Take the growbay's spare racks

outcome.narrative: The spare racks come out of the growbay and go onto the hull. The crop loses its overflow trays and some of its light, and shows it within the day. The hull shows the patch. The botanist, if aboard, shows nothing at all, which is worse.

choices.text: Rework the load paths instead

outcome.narrative: {crew.engineer} spends days with the structural drawings and a torque wrench, shifting load off the damaged panels onto frames that can take it, and bolts on nothing new at all. The hull is stronger without a single partition coming down. Nobody quite understands how. The engineer is happy to explain, at length.

choices.text: Leave the ship in one piece

outcome.narrative: You leave everything bolted where it is. The partitions stay up, the racks stay full and the galley table stays a galley table. The hull stays exactly as thin as it was, and the list stays on the screen, in case.

title: Cash Welds

ai_flavor.aria: A WELDER! With a SIGN! ARIA trusts anyone who writes their prices in marker!
ai_flavor.marv: MARV has examined the welder's work on the ship two berths down. It is good. MARV is mildly annoyed by this.
ai_flavor.rex: REX rates the welder a low threat and a high skill. He would like to know where they learned. He suspects the answer is a war.
ai_flavor.chip: CHIP must warn that unlicensed welds void your StellarSeal™ hull warranty! Your warranty was voided some time ago! CHIP mentions it for completeness!
ai_flavor.ajoy: AJOY has watched the apprentice for a while. Their welds are better than the sign suggests. Slower, but better. She mentions it before you pay full price out of habit.

body:
In the berth next to yours, a welder with a home-built rig and a hand-lettered sign is doing hull work for cash, no questions asked.

The sign says WELDS. Underneath, smaller: CHEAPER THAN THE YARD. Underneath that, smaller still and added later: APPRENTICES HALF PRICE.

The welder has looked your hull up and down, sucked their teeth, and named a price. It is lower than the yard's. It is not lower than nothing.

choices.text: Pay for the full job

outcome.narrative: The welder works through two station nights, fast and neat and smoking slightly, and by the second morning the worst of your hull is new steel. They take the money, tip their mask and are already eyeing the next berth. It is honestly good work. You check it twice anyway.

choices.text: Pay the welder in fuel

outcome.narrative: The welder runs their rig off a fuel cell and is always short. You pump some of yours across, and they patch the worst of it for that, quickly and well. The hull is better, the tank is lighter, and everyone at the berth agrees this is how things used to be done.

choices.text: Let the apprentice practice on you

outcome.narrative: The apprentice is keen, slow, and learning on your ship. The welds go on one careful bead at a time, some of them twice, while the calendar ticks over in the berth. The hull ends up sound. The apprentice ends up good at it. The days end up gone.

choices.text: Thank them and move on

outcome.narrative: You thank the welder and leave the sign behind. The yard will charge more and do it properly, or you will fly on as you are. The welder shrugs and goes back to their coffee. They have seen ships like yours come back.

title: License to Seal

ai_flavor.aria: The foam has a MASCOT! He's so happy! ARIA is sure he would let us use the foam if he could!
ai_flavor.marv: MARV has read the license terms. The canister is ours. The foam inside it is not. MARV finds this the most honest thing a company has ever told him.
ai_flavor.rex: REX has a solution for the license lock. It involves the lock no longer existing. He is waiting for permission.
ai_flavor.chip: CHIP is thrilled to see a SealRight™ product in the field! CHIP can renew your license instantly! CHIP earns a small commission on renewals! The law says CHIP has to mention that!
ai_flavor.ajoy: AJOY has been in the SealRight™ customer care queue before. They do answer, eventually. Eventually is eight days. She mentions it so nobody can say she didn't.

body:
The emergency locker holds a canister of SealRight™ expanding hull foam. Spray it on a damaged panel and it sets in seconds into something harder than the panel was.

The canister will not spray. A small screen on the nozzle explains that SealRight™ is a licensed product, that the license lapsed when the ship's previous owner stopped paying, and that dispensing will resume upon renewal. There is a code to scan. There is a smiling foam mascot.

The hull, meanwhile, is not getting any less damaged.

choices.text: Renew the license

outcome.narrative: You scan the code, accept the terms without reading them, and pay. The nozzle's screen lights up, the mascot gives a thumbs-up, and the foam goes on thick and sets hard over the worst of the damage. It is, irritatingly, an excellent product. A receipt arrives. So does a newsletter.

choices.text: Crack the license lock

outcome.narrative: You pry the cover off the nozzle and talk the license chip into believing it is a much older, much more trusting chip. It believes you. The foam goes on and sets hard. Somewhere, a compliance server logs one canister as 'missing, presumed liberated'.

choices.text: Open a ticket with customer care

outcome.narrative: You open a ticket with SealRight™ customer care and wait. And wait. Days into the queue a cheerful agent grants a one-time courtesy unlock 'for a valued customer', and the foam goes on at last, thick and hard and excellent. You have been a valued customer for days. It felt longer.

choices.text: Jam the whole canister in the worst hole

outcome.narrative: You wedge the whole canister, license lock and mascot and all, into the worst of the damage and weld a strap over it. It is not a repair. It is a very expensive bung. It holds. The mascot smiles out at the stars from the hull for the rest of the voyage.

title: Shore Leave

ai_flavor.aria: GROUND! Real ground! ARIA wants everyone to roll in it! In suits! Responsibly!
ai_flavor.marv: MARV has the suit reserves, the schedule and the morale curve on one screen. Two of them argue against going down. MARV is not saying which one he agrees with.
ai_flavor.rex: REX has swept the landing zone. It contains rocks, dust and no threats. He recommends shore leave in the voice he uses for ordering an advance.
ai_flavor.chip: CHIP notes that ShoreLeave™ is a paid-tier crew benefit! You are on the free tier! The free tier includes looking at it!
ai_flavor.ajoy: AJOY says proper days down there cost four, and walks in suits cost two. She'd pay the four. She suggested paying it a while back, for the record, when the morale curve was less of a cliff.

body:
Below the ship is real ground: rock and dust and an actual horizon under a sky, the first anyone aboard has seen in a long time.

The crew has been standing at the viewport without saying much. Nobody has asked to go down. Every face is asking.

The ship computer notes that the surface is survivable in suits, that the schedule is tight, and that morale is the lowest it has recorded this voyage.

choices.text: Give them a few proper days on the surface

outcome.narrative: You set the ship down and let them out. Mostly, they walk. Somebody throws a rock as far as it will go and somebody else measures it. Someone lies on their back in the dust and looks at the sky all afternoon. It costs days. Nobody who went down would trade them back.

choices.text: Short walks in suits, close to the ship

outcome.narrative: Two days of short walks in suits: loops around the ship and back to the airlock before the suit tanks run low, refilled each time from the ship's own air. It is not much. It is boots on the ground and a horizon, and the crew comes back in quieter, in the good way.

choices.text: The pilot flies them low over it

outcome.narrative: {crew.pilot} takes the ship down low and flies the long way round the valley, slow and steady, while everyone crowds the viewports. Nobody leaves the ship. Nobody needs to. It is the best flying anyone aboard has ever seen, and the pilot knows it.

choices.text: No time. Keep to the schedule

outcome.narrative: You keep the schedule. The ship lifts without anyone setting foot outside, and the crew watches the horizon curve away into the black. Nobody complains. That is not the same thing as nobody minding.

title: Work to Rule

ai_flavor.aria: Everyone is following the RULES! ARIA loves rules! ARIA is beginning to see why other people don't!
ai_flavor.marv: MARV has timed the filter change. It took the whole morning, exactly as specified. MARV has never seen the manual followed before. He finds it more frightening than mutiny.
ai_flavor.rex: REX knows a work-to-rule when he sees one. He has seen one break a garrison. He has also seen one ended by somebody listening. He recommends the second.
ai_flavor.chip: CHIP notes that the Crew Grievance Procedure™ requires a reply within a set number of business days! There are no business days in space! CHIP is checking whether that helps you or them!
ai_flavor.ajoy: AJOY has read the list. Every item on it is fair. She'd start with the food. She knows you know that.

body:
The crew has not gone on strike. The crew has gone by the book.

Every task aboard is now done exactly as the manual describes, no faster, with every optional safety check performed and every form filed in triplicate. A filter change takes a morning. A course correction needs a signed request. The galley closes for the mandated rest period, which nobody knew existed until today.

Nobody has said why. Everybody knows why. A list of grievances has been left, very correctly, in your in-tray.

choices.text: Meet them on the food

outcome.narrative: You agree to the first item on the list: real meals again, generous ones, starting tonight. The galley reopens with a feast that eats {cost.food} points of food, and the rations stay at PIG OUT after it. The manual goes back on the shelf, and the ship gets faster at everything. The stores will feel it.

choices.text: Pay a bonus from the ship's account

outcome.narrative: You pay a bonus from the ship's account, equal shares, no conditions. It does not fix the list. It does say you read it. By evening the forms are gone, and the filters change in minutes again.

choices.text: Let the diplomat take the list

outcome.narrative: {crew.diplomat} takes the list, takes over the mess table, and takes two days going through every item with everyone, until each has an answer, even if it is not the one they wanted. It is exhausting for everybody. It works. The manual goes back on the shelf.

choices.text: Ride it out by the book

outcome.narrative: You let them work to rule, and do the same yourself. Everything aboard takes as long as the manual says it should, which is a very long time, and the voyage loses days it did not have. Somewhere in the slow stretch the anger runs out on its own. The crew is rested. The schedule is not.

title: Game Night

ai_flavor.aria: A GAME! With RULES! Pages of them! ARIA has a strategy already! It is called 'trust everyone'!
ai_flavor.marv: MARV has read the rules. They contain a loop that would let a game last forever. MARV has told no one. MARV suspects that is the point.
ai_flavor.rex: REX has played. REX won, by never trading with anybody. Nobody will play with REX any more. REX considers this a strategic victory.
ai_flavor.chip: CHIP notes the game closely resembles Commerce™, a registered product! CHIP will overlook it in exchange for a mention in the rules! THE AUDITOR is a good start!
ai_flavor.ajoy: AJOY isn't allowed to play, on account of seeing every hand. She is refereeing instead. She has already overruled the captain twice, in advance.

body:
Someone has invented a board game.

It is played on the navigation table, with ration-brick wrappers for tiles, bolts for pieces, and rules that run to several pages and are still being argued over. It involves trading, betrayal, and a card called THE AUDITOR that nobody wants to draw. Nobody has finished a game yet. Everyone wants to.

They have asked whether the captain would like to play.

choices.text: Pull up a chair

outcome.narrative: You play. You lose, badly, to an alliance that forms and dissolves around you in the space of a single hand, and you draw THE AUDITOR at the worst possible moment. It is the best evening anyone can remember. It runs on into the next day, the work waits, and the ship does not seem to mind.

choices.text: Print them a proper set

outcome.narrative: The fabricator turns out a proper board, real tiles and a little gray AUDITOR holding a clipboard. It puts some wear on the fabricator. The crew treats the set like an heirloom, and the bolts go back where they belong.

choices.text: Put up a prize from the galley

outcome.narrative: You put up a prize: the winner takes the good tin from the galley, the one everybody has been saving. The stakes turn a game into a tournament. The tin goes, {cost.food} points of food and worth every one of them, and the winner shares it anyway, which is how you know it worked.

choices.text: Let them play; keep the watch yourself

outcome.narrative: You leave them to it and keep the watch yourself. The game runs late, and from the bridge you can see the light in the mess stay on long past the end of shift. In the morning everyone is tired, and slightly better.
